attacks.name: transient_decline_world_documented_cadence
attacks.probes: A36 + A31 + A8 + A15 + A34 — in a world dominated by transient issuer-side declines, the recovery signal is TIME-SINCE-FAILURE, not time-until-salary. The adaptive policy's core lever (defer to the next predicted income event) is a pure latency cost here, while Razorpay's documented T+1/T+2/T+3 cadence is exactly the right instrument for declines that clear within hours. Stable balances remove the funds signal, mild congestion removes the window signal, and a near-harmless undelivered multiplier removes the notification signal, so adaptive has nothing left to be smart about but still pays for waiting.
attacks.plausibility: Indian issuer estates run overnight batch/EOD windows and periodic core-banking maintenance; a large share of 'declines' are soft, issuer-side, and clear by the next morning — which is precisely why the published cadence is next-day, next-day, next-day.

attacks.name: noise_defeats_point_prediction
attacks.probes: A13 + A15 + A16 + A1/A2 — the adaptive policy is a point estimator of 'when will this account have money'; the [3,7,14] baseline is a diversified sampler of the same distribution. Push irregular income to the top of its declared range and spending volatility to its maximum, and the point estimate degrades faster than the sampler does. Crucially, revocation is set to its PATIENT end (4), which removes the handicap their early_revocation scenario silently imposed on multi-attempt baselines, so the baseline gets to spend all four attempts across a 24-day spread.
attacks.plausibility: Gig, cash-wage and small-trader income in India is lumpy and UPI-spend volatility is high; predicting the balance on a named future date for such an account is materially harder than simply sampling four different dates across a month.

attacks.name: escalation_race_fast_baseline_asks_first
attacks.probes: A35 + A20 + A1 — escalation is a SHARED channel, and the harness treats the response rate as symmetric, but it is not symmetric in TIME. A baseline on the documented [1] cadence exhausts its 4-attempt cap by T+3 and reaches the customer with a pay-link on day 3; an adaptive policy that holds attempts back for predicted income events reaches the same channel two to three weeks later. Set escalation to its optimistic rate and its fastest lag and the fast, dumb policy monetises the strongest recovery mechanism in the model first — while patient customers (revocation at 4) never punish it for burning attempts.
attacks.plausibility: In practice most Indian recurring-payment recovery is not won by retry timing at all; it is won by a WhatsApp/SMS payment link that the customer taps — and the merchant who sends that link on day 3 beats the one who sends it on day 21, especially before the next billing cycle's dunning noise.

attacks.name: short_validity_punishes_patience
attacks.probes: A32 + A36 + A35 — the adaptive policy buys success probability with calendar time, and this scenario prices that time. Mandate validity is pinned to the bottom of its declared range (180 days) while expired mandates are a fifth of the failure mix, so a long recovery arc has a materially higher chance of landing on an already-dead mandate. Escalation is pinned pessimistic and slow, so the adaptive policy's fallback cannot rescue the attempts it deferred.
attacks.plausibility: Plenty of Indian UPI Autopay and card mandates are registered for a 6-month or 12-month term tied to the subscription/SIP term rather than in perpetuity, so a failure occurring near the end of that term genuinely leaves only days of head-room, not weeks.

attacks.name: ceiling_effect_everything_recovers
attacks.probes: A15 + A8 + A17/A34 + A1 — this attacks the LIFT rather than the level. With slow decay, low volatility, a mostly-salaried population, mild congestion and near-harmless undelivered notifications, almost every recoverable failure is recoverable by ANY policy that tries again within a fortnight. The [3,7,14] baseline already does that, so both policies saturate against the recoverable-only denominator and the +10% advantage has nowhere to come from. This is the scenario where the claim is not false but empty.
attacks.plausibility: Salaried metro customers with a maintained minimum balance and a single OTT/SIP mandate are a large, real segment; for them a mid-month retry is nearly as good as a payday retry, which is exactly why generic backoff has survived in production for so long.

attacks.name: high_ticket_otp_wall_drowns_the_money_headline
attacks.probes: A22 + A33 + A6 + A35 — the ₹-recovered headline, not the recovery rate. Push the amount mixture to the EMI/SIP-heavy end of its declared ranges so a large share of mandate value sits above the ₹15,000 no-OTP ceiling, where no retry-timing intelligence can help: those debits need customer authentication, i.e. escalation. Pin escalation to its pessimistic rate and slowest lag and the money metric is dominated by a channel where both policies score near zero, while adaptive's timing wins accrue only on ₹99–₹999 OTT mandates.
attacks.plausibility: EMI and larger SIP mandates routinely exceed ₹15,000 and therefore fall outside the AFA-exempt band, so in a real book the rupees are concentrated exactly where retry timing has the least authority.

attacks.name: two_of_three_levers_nulled
attacks.probes: A8 + A17 + A34 + A36 — the adaptive policy has three claimed sources of edge: congestion-window avoidance, notification-aware scheduling, and income-event timing. Here the first is nulled (degradation at its floor, so avoiding 10:00–13:00 buys almost nothing) and the second is nulled behaviourally (undelivered notifications barely change the outcome even at the maximum delivery-failure rate), while congestion and notification failures are made a HALF of the failure mix. Adaptive is therefore spending its scheduling freedom on the two largest failure classes it cannot influence, and paying 24h notification-to-debit latency for the privilege.
attacks.plausibility: NPCI execution windows shift queueing and latency more than terminal success, and Indian customers with autopay mandates typically see the debit in their PSP app regardless of whether the SMS landed — so both effects being small at once is an entirely ordinary state of the world, not a contrivance.

attacks.name: no_signal_world_compound_corner
attacks.probes: Joint A13 + A15 + A36 + A31 + A8 + A34 + A32 + A35 + A2 — every parameter is inside its declared range, but the corner was never visited because the sweep was one-at-a-time. Simultaneously: the population has minimal exploitable phase (irregular at its cap), balances are maximally noisy, the failure mix is transient-technical-heavy at the top of its base rate, congestion and notification effects are at their harmless ends, mandate validity is at its floor, escalation is slow and weak, revocation is patient (so the baseline is never punished for spending attempts), and the baseline runs its strongest documented-alternative spread. There is no signal left for the adaptive policy to condition on, and its only remaining differentiators — waiting and escalating — are both priced badly.
attacks.plausibility: None of these settings is exotic on its own; a sub-portfolio of gig-income customers on a bank with a flaky core, holding 6-month mandates, is a segment a payments engineer could name — and the whole point of a sensitivity claim is that it must survive the joint corner, not just the marginals.
